title: RCMP didn't try to de-escalate in fatal shooting of Eastern Passage man: witness
article: She had no clue why more than a dozen rifle-carrying RCMP officers had converged on her neighbour Richard Wheeler.
On Monday morning, four days after the 60-year-old man and father was fatally shot by RCMP in Eastern Passage, the woman fought back tears recounting Wheeler's last moments.
The deadly encounter lasted between 20 and 30 seconds, she said.
The woman, who asked not be identified, said she is still in shock and trying to process what she saw.
The woman said she was at her Howard Avenue home Thursday afternoon when she spotted a team of RCMP officers "creeping" up her street at about 4:25 p.m. with rifles ready to fire.
The woman said she saw Wheeler step outside the side entrance of his home and sit down on the steps below, about 10 seconds before the officers bore down on him.

"He was sitting on the side steps where he always sits and they were coming from all angles, 10 to 15 officers," said the woman. "They were coming from behind the house, they came from around the house next door, from the street, and all of them were armed with rifles."
"They yelled, 'Put the gun down Richard,' or 'Put your hands up Richard,' I'm not sure which because it happened so fast."

She said Wheeler responded by lighting a cigarette and then pulled a gun out from his waist area. Right at that point, the officers opened fire. She recalled hearing at least two gunshots and the confrontation lasting between 20 to 30 seconds.

The RCMP issued a news release last Thursday evening saying that officers responded to a call of a man armed with a handgun uttering threats at an Eastern Passage residence. RCMP said officers attempted to de-escalate before shooting Wheeler. The woman said none of the officers attempted to calm the situation. She said their actions had the opposite effect.
"They went in guns blazing, pretty well," said the woman. "I was home all day and I didn't hear any noise coming from the house. Nothing out of the ordinary happened."
She described Wheeler as quiet. He kept to himself and never behaved violently, she said.

Another neighbour, who lives a few doors down from Wheeler's home, said he also spotted officers with rifles in the neighbourhood Thursday afternoon. The man, who also didn't want to provide his name, said he had been friends with Wheeler for more than 30 years and never knew him to be violent.
"(Police) were all over the neighbourhood and I thought, what the hell is going on?" he said. "It seemed like they were on a mission."

Both neighbours said Wheeler had a significant alcohol addiction and mental health problems. He was also battling cancer, they said. The man said Wheeler had gotten into trouble with the law related to his drinking but offered no details on his offences.
But he said Wheeler had attempted to get help.
"He had told me many times that he tried to get mental health support, but, boy, there's next to no help out there in this province, is there? But Richard was looking for help and he wanted help."

Cpl. Jennifer Clarke, Nova Scotia RCMP spokeswoman, wouldn't say how, specifically, officers tried to de-escalate their encounter with Wheeler. Clarke said officers also used verbal commands trying to disarm the suspected but that he was "absolutely not responsive to that."

Clarke said only RCMP national headquarters in Ottawa could provide information on training programs for officers. On Monday, the Chronicle Herald inquired with RCMP headquarters for information on de-escalation training for officers and policies around lethal use of force, but did not get a response.

Halifax RCMP has access to the Mental Health Mobile Crisis Team, which includes a police officer and mental health clinician. Clarke couldn't say whether a request was put in for the team's assistance. But she also said the group wouldn't be part of the initial response in a situation like the incident on Thursday.
"Public safety is absolutely number one," said Clarke. "There are a number of calls where they can assist. That's not one of them."
The Serious Incident Response Team, the province's independent police watchdog agency, is investigating the incident.
On Monday Felix Cacchione would provide no details about the shooting.
The RCMP media release on Thursday indicated more than one officer opened fire on Wheeler. But neither Cacchione or Clarke would confirm that.
Over the weekend, Wheeler's son and daughter posted on their Facebook pages that their father had a pellet gun on him when he was fatally shot. Clarke would not confirm whether that was the case.

The female neighbour is questioning why the incident didn't prompt RCMP to issue a public alert, given the number of officers that responded. She said none of the officers involved warned her or anybody else on the street she spoke to of the situation as it unfolded. She said she asked two officers why no alert was issued. She said one replied there wasn't enough time, another said an alert was being planned.
Clarke said an alert was not suitable for the incident, but would offer no additional comment.
Another neighbour of Wheeler's lamented his friend's death but supported the actions of the police. The man, who also did not want to be identified, said he had never had any problems with Wheeler.
"I was friends with Richard, absolutely, but the cops did what they had to do and that was it," he said. "It seems like they had no choice."
